Lesson 3 of 3

Concurrency follow-ups and bridging into scale

Handle common interviewer pivots around thread safety, shared state, and how an object design changes once the system has to scale out.

25-35 min LLD flow Machine coding, testing, and follow-up handling 4 guided stops

Why this lesson matters

Strong candidates can explain not only the object model but also what breaks when multiple callers race, shared state grows hot, or the design must move from in-memory logic to distributed coordination.

Start with this framing

Interview framing

Strong candidates can explain not only the object model but also what breaks when multiple callers race, shared state grows hot, or the design must move from in-memory logic to distributed coordination.

What to say first

  • Point out shared mutable state and contention risks.

    Show likely answer
    • Point out shared mutable state and contention risks.
    • Strong candidates can explain not only the object model but also what breaks when multiple callers race, shared state grows hot, or the design must move from in-memory logic to distributed coordination.
    • Claiming thread safety without naming the shared state being protected.

  • Explain what remains local logic versus distributed infrastructure.

    Show likely answer
    • Explain what remains local logic versus distributed infrastructure.
    • Explain which parts remain local object logic and which must evolve into durable storage, queues, or distributed coordination once a single process is no longer enough.
    • Strong candidates can explain not only the object model but also what breaks when multiple callers race, shared state grows hot, or the design must move from in-memory logic to distributed coordination.

  • Describe the first design seam that changes under scale.

    Show likely answer
    • Describe the first design seam that changes under scale.
    • Interview follow-ups should extend the current design. Avoid rewriting everything; instead explain the seam or responsibility that changes as scale increases.
    • Strong candidates can explain not only the object model but also what breaks when multiple callers race, shared state grows hot, or the design must move from in-memory logic to distributed coordination.

Identify shared mutable state

Find the objects or caches that multiple threads or requests may touch concurrently and decide whether to lock, partition, copy, or serialize access.

Common pitfalls

What to avoid

  • Claiming thread safety without naming the shared state being protected.
  • Jumping from local object design straight to full distributed architecture with no bridge.
  • Throwing away the original design instead of extending it.
